subject: Dedicated capacity: headroom carveout & queueing behavior request
messages:
From: Liam O'Connor <liam.oconnor@horizons-health.com>
To: Stephanie Nguyen <stephanie_nguyen@redwood.com>
Date: 2025-09-14T09:12:00-07:00
Subject: Request: dedicated capacity latency guardrail & headroom carveout

Hi Stephanie,

Thanks for taking the quick intro last week. Horizons Health is moving a set of inference endpoints for clinical triage into production in Q4 and we expect sustained traffic during 08:00-20:00 ET. Two pain points we need to address before committing to a reserved pool:

- Tail latency during concurrent nightly batch jobs: our models are sensitive to 99th percentile latency spikes. We need clarity on behavior when background batch jobs run in the same pool.
- Headroom guarantees: during our busiest hours we need a defined short-term headroom (e.g., a burst token pool or soft preemption carveout) so we don't degrade user-facing SLAs.

Can Redwood provide an operational carveout and binding language describing queueing behavior and any credit/headroom mechanism? Also please share a draft amendment we can circulate with procurement.

CC'ing ops@horizons-health.com for scheduling.

Appreciate it — happy to jump on a 30m call next week.

Best,
Liam O'Connor
VP Product Ops
Horizons Health
From: Stephanie Nguyen <stephanie_nguyen@redwood.com>
To: Liam O'Connor <liam.oconnor@horizons-health.com>
Cc: Ben Carter <ben_carter@redwood.com>
Date: 2025-09-14T11:05:00-07:00
Subject: Re: Request: dedicated capacity latency guardrail & headroom carveout

Hi Liam — thanks, this is exactly the kind of scenario we built Redwood Dedicated for.

Quick summary / next steps:
- We can propose a "soft-headroom" policy: short-lived burst tokens reserved for business-hour traffic that avoid preemption for a configurable window (default 120s).
- For batch/backfill jobs we recommend a separate nightly tenant or strictly scheduled windows; if co-located, we provide queueing priority lanes and documented eviction order.
- I'll assemble a draft SLA amendment for your procurement team and a short runbook describing queueing behavior.

Ben — can you and I pull together a clean amendment and an ops playbook (SLA_questionnaire.xlsx attached) so Horizons has something to review?

Liam — can you share the expected QPS profile during 08:00-20:00 ET and an example spike pattern? That will help us size headroom tokens.

Thanks,
Stephanie Nguyen
Director, Customer Success — Redwood Inference
stephanie_nguyen@redwood.com
From: Ben Carter <ben_carter@redwood.com>
To: Stephanie Nguyen <stephanie_nguyen@redwood.com>, Evelyn Hart <evelyn_hart@redwood.com>
Date: 2025-09-15T09:30:00-07:00
Subject: Re: Request: dedicated capacity latency guardrail & headroom carveout

Stephanie / Evelyn — attaching draft amendment and a short pricing note. Highlights:
- Headroom token pool: configurable by commitment tier; default 5% of committed capacity for 2-minute bursts; can be increased for an incremental fee.
- Queueing lanes: guaranteed priority for "interactive" traffic during declared business hours; batch jobs get a lower priority class and a maximum concurrency budget.
- Credits: where we miss the defined 99th percentile targets due to platform behavior (not customer misconfiguration), we propose a token crediting mechanism (one token = 1% monthly bill up to 10% cap).

Attachment: redwood-dedicated-sla-amendment-draft.pdf
Also noted potential procurement concerns around auditability of priority enforcement — we'll include observability hooks for token consumption and eviction events.

Ben Carter
Enterprise Lead, Redwood Inference
ben_carter@redwood.com
From: Stephanie Nguyen <stephanie_nguyen@redwood.com>
To: Liam O'Connor <liam.oconnor@horizons-health.com>
Cc: Ben Carter <ben_carter@redwood.com>, Evelyn Hart <evelyn_hart@redwood.com>
Date: 2025-09-16T08:42:00-07:00
Subject: Re: Request: dedicated capacity latency guardrail & headroom carveout

Liam — attaching our proposed amendment and a short ops playbook excerpt. Key items called out in the draft:

- Operational definitions: what counts as "interactive" vs "batch", how we compute 99th percentile (sliding 30-day window), and the headroom token lifecycle.
- Enforcement and observability: token consumption events are streamed to your observability endpoint; we also provide per-tenant traces for eviction and preemption events.
- Credits and remediation: if Redwood's routing/queueing behavior causes a breach of the agreed 99th percentile target during business hours, we will issue credits per the formula in Section 4.2.

Proposal: 60-minute review call on Wednesday 2025-09-17 11:00 ET to walk procurement/infra through the draft. If that works, I'll send a calendar invite.

Attachments: redwood-dedicated-sla-amendment-draft.pdf, SLA_questionnaire.xlsx
DocuSign preview: https://docusign.com/packet/0a9f2e
HubSpot: https://app.hubspot.com/contacts/123456/company/8342

Looking forward to next steps.

Best,
Stephanie Nguyen
Director, Customer Success — Redwood Inference
From: Liam O'Connor <liam.oconnor@horizons-health.com>
To: Stephanie Nguyen <stephanie_nguyen@redwood.com>
Cc: ops@horizons-health.com
Date: 2025-09-16T16:24:00-07:00
Subject: Re: Request: dedicated capacity latency guardrail & headroom carveout

Stephanie — thanks for the quick turnaround and the draft. A few quick pieces from our side:

- We'll review the amendment with procurement; initial flag: we need clearer language around the measurement window for 99th percentile during "incident" windows (we prefer a 1-hour micro-window carveout for spikes caused by external upstreams).
- Proof-of-concept ask: could Redwood stand up a short 48-hour validation with the proposed token config so we can validate behavior under our load?
- Credit ask: if the headroom fails because of platform-level scheduling (not our misconfig), we'd like the first failure to trigger a one-time service credit equivalent to 10% of that hour's bill and a post-mortem within 48 hours.

I can join the Wednesday call if you add a short POC agenda item.
